Topics.Title: Foreign Keys and Identity Columns Fundamentals
Topics.Summary: Explains the challenge of inserting data across tables linked by foreign keys and how SQL Server identity columns automatically generate unique primary key values. Covers IDENTITY(seed, increment) syntax, custom seeds, and why identity gaps occur.

Elements.Title: The Foreign Key Insert Challenge
Elements.BodyText: Relational databases link tables through foreign keys, which creates an ordering problem when inserting new data. A parent row must exist before any child row that references it can be inserted.
Elements.Notes: Classic example: an order must be inserted first so its OrderID exists, and only then can order line items referencing that OrderID be added.

Items.Text: Insert order: parent tables first (Customers, Products), then dependents (Orders, Addresses), then OrderItems.
The parent's primary key is generated by the database, so the application does not know it in advance.
The generated key must be captured and passed to the child INSERT as the foreign key value.
Stored procedures encapsulate this multi-step workflow atomically, keeping application code simple.
A dependency hierarchy helps: Level 0 = Customers/Products, Level 1 = Orders/Addresses, Level 2 = OrderItems.

Elements.Title: Why Use Identity Columns
Elements.BodyText: An identity column tells SQL Server to generate a unique numeric value for each new row automatically. This removes the burden of key generation from application code.
Elements.Notes: Identity columns are the standard choice for surrogate primary keys in SQL Server.

Items.Text: Automatic generation: SQL Server produces unique values with no application input.
Performance: identity generation is optimized for high-volume inserts.
Simplicity: no custom ID generation or lookup logic needed in the application.
Consistency: uniqueness is guaranteed within the table.
Concurrency: multiple simultaneous inserts are handled safely without collisions.

Elements.Title: IDENTITY(seed, increment) Syntax
Elements.BodyText: The IDENTITY property is declared on a single numeric column and takes two arguments: the seed (starting value) and the increment (step size). It is typically paired with PRIMARY KEY.
Elements.Notes: Example: OrderID INT IDENTITY(1,1) PRIMARY KEY produces 1, 2, 3, 4 ...

Items.Text: IDENTITY(1,1) is the most common form, producing 1, 2, 3, 4 and so on.
The seed is the value assigned to the very first row inserted.
The increment is added to the previous identity value for each subsequent row.
Only one identity column is permitted per table.
Identity values cannot be supplied directly in an INSERT unless IDENTITY_INSERT is enabled.

Elements.Title: Custom Seeds and Increments
Elements.BodyText: Seed and increment values can be customized to meet business or formatting requirements. This is useful when IDs must start at a particular number or follow a stepped pattern.
Elements.Notes: Starting product IDs at 1000 avoids short, ambiguous numbers in customer-facing catalogs.

Items.Text: IDENTITY(1000,1) on Products starts the sequence at 1000, 1001, 1002 ...
IDENTITY(1,10) on BatchJobs produces 1, 11, 21, 31 ... leaving room between values.
Larger seeds can prevent collisions when merging data from multiple systems.
The pattern is fixed at table creation and applies to every subsequent insert.

Elements.Title: Identity Gaps Are Normal
Elements.BodyText: Identity values are consumed when generated and are never reused, so the sequence can contain gaps. This is expected behavior, not a defect.
Elements.Notes: Treat identity values as opaque unique keys, not as a reliable row counter.

Items.Text: A rolled-back transaction still consumes the identity value it generated.
Deleted rows leave permanent holes in the numbering.
Failed inserts and server restarts can also create gaps.
Never rely on identity values being contiguous or using them to count rows.
If a strictly gapless sequence is required, it must be implemented with other mechanisms.

Elements.Title: Identity Columns in the Example Schema
Elements.BodyText: The e-commerce schema uses identity columns on every primary key and foreign key constraints to link the tables. This setup illustrates why retrieving generated identity values matters.
Elements.Notes: Each child table's foreign key column is a plain INT that must receive a value generated by its parent's identity column.

Items.Text: Customers and Products are Level 0 tables with IDENTITY(1,1) primary keys and no dependencies.
Orders has FK_Orders_Customers referencing Customers(CustomerID).
Addresses has FK_Addresses_Customers referencing Customers(CustomerID).
OrderItems depends on both Orders and Products via two foreign key constraints.
Because keys are generated at insert time, special functions are required to retrieve them before inserting child rows.

Topics.Title: Retrieving Generated Identity Values
Topics.Summary: Compares SCOPE_IDENTITY(), @@IDENTITY, IDENT_CURRENT(), and the OUTPUT clause for capturing newly generated keys. Highlights scope, trigger safety, and concurrency implications so learners choose the correct method for each situation.

Elements.Title: Why You Need Identity Retrieval Functions
Elements.BodyText: Identity columns let SQL Server automatically generate unique sequential keys, but the generated value is not returned to you by the INSERT statement itself. To use a new key as a foreign key in a child table, you must explicitly capture it.
Elements.Notes: Example: inserting an Order generates OrderID, which must then be supplied when inserting rows into OrderItems. Identity values are never reused after a rollback, so gaps in the sequence are normal and expected.

Items.Text: Identity columns are defined with IDENTITY(seed, increment), such as IDENTITY(1,1) or IDENTITY(1000,1).
SQL Server handles uniqueness and concurrency for identity generation automatically.
The newly generated value must be captured immediately after the INSERT, before other statements run.
Choosing the wrong retrieval method can silently return the wrong key and corrupt referential integrity.

Elements.Title: SCOPE_IDENTITY() — The Recommended Default
Elements.BodyText: SCOPE_IDENTITY() returns the last identity value generated within the current scope — the current stored procedure, trigger, function, or batch. This makes it the safest general-purpose choice for single-row inserts.
Elements.Notes: Typical pattern: INSERT INTO Orders (...) VALUES (...); DECLARE @NewOrderID INT = SCOPE_IDENTITY();

Items.Text: It is both trigger-safe and concurrency-safe because it is limited to the executing scope.
Use it immediately after the INSERT and assign it to a local variable or OUTPUT parameter.
It is the standard choice in stored procedures such as usp_InsertCustomer and usp_InsertOrder.
It returns NULL if no identity value has been generated in the current scope.

Elements.Title: @@IDENTITY — Use With Caution
Elements.BodyText: @@IDENTITY returns the last identity value generated anywhere in the current session, regardless of scope. This makes it vulnerable to returning a value produced by a trigger rather than by your own INSERT.
Elements.Notes: Older teaching examples, such as the Music Database sp_InsertSong procedure, use @@IDENTITY; modern code should replace these calls with SCOPE_IDENTITY().

Items.Text: If an INSERT trigger writes to an audit or log table with its own identity column, @@IDENTITY returns that trigger's value.
It is session-scoped, so it is concurrency-safe but not trigger-safe.
Treat it as legacy syntax that is acceptable to read but not to write in new code.
Using @@IDENTITY instead of SCOPE_IDENTITY() is listed among the most common stored procedure pitfalls.

Elements.Title: IDENT_CURRENT() — Table-Specific and Risky
Elements.BodyText: IDENT_CURRENT('TableName') returns the last identity value generated for a specific table across all sessions and scopes. Because it ignores who generated the value, it is unsafe for retrieving a key you just inserted.
Elements.Notes: Example: SELECT IDENT_CURRENT('Orders') AS LastOrderID;

Items.Text: Another user's concurrent insert can change the value between your INSERT and your read.
It is not concurrency-safe and should never be used to populate foreign keys.
Its legitimate uses are monitoring, reporting, and checking the current seed of a table.
It works without having performed any insert in the current session.

Elements.Title: The OUTPUT Clause — Most Flexible
Elements.BodyText: The OUTPUT clause captures values directly from the rows affected by an INSERT, using the inserted pseudo-table. It is the only reliable option when a single statement inserts multiple rows.
Elements.Notes: Pattern: DECLARE @InsertedOrders TABLE (OrderID INT); INSERT INTO Orders (...) OUTPUT inserted.OrderID INTO @InsertedOrders VALUES (...);

Items.Text: It is statement-scoped, trigger-safe, and concurrency-safe.
It can return multiple columns — including computed columns such as LineTotal — not just the identity key.
Results can be streamed back to the caller or captured into a table variable for later use.
In application code, OUTPUT INSERTED.CustomerID with ExecuteScalar() returns the new key in one round-trip.

Elements.Title: Choosing the Right Method
Elements.BodyText: Each method differs in scope, trigger safety, and concurrency safety, so the correct choice depends on whether you are inserting one row or many and whether triggers exist on the table.
Elements.Notes: Summary: SCOPE_IDENTITY() = current scope; @@IDENTITY = session; IDENT_CURRENT() = table across all sessions; OUTPUT = statement.

Items.Text: Use SCOPE_IDENTITY() for single-row inserts inside stored procedures.
Use the OUTPUT clause for multi-row inserts or when you need several columns returned.
Avoid @@IDENTITY in new code because triggers can make it return the wrong value.
Never use IDENT_CURRENT() to retrieve a just-inserted ID under concurrent load.
Verify in testing that identity values are returned correctly, including under concurrent execution scenarios.

Topics.Title: Designing the Schema and Dependency Order
Topics.Summary: Walks through a complete e-commerce schema (Customers, Products, Orders, OrderItems, Addresses) with its foreign key constraints. Introduces dependency-level thinking to determine the correct order of inserts across related tables.

Elements.Title: The E-Commerce Schema at a Glance
Elements.BodyText: The working example for this module is a five-table e-commerce schema: Customers, Products, Orders, OrderItems, and Addresses. Each table uses an INT IDENTITY(1,1) primary key so SQL Server generates surrogate keys automatically.
Elements.Notes: This schema is deliberately small but contains every relationship pattern you will encounter: independent lookup tables, one-to-many parent/child links, and a child that depends on two parents.

Items.Text: Customers holds FirstName, LastName, Email, and a CreatedDate defaulted to GETDATE().
Products holds ProductName, Description, UnitPrice, and StockQuantity.
Orders records CustomerID, OrderDate, TotalAmount, and Status.
OrderItems records OrderID, ProductID, Quantity, UnitPrice, and a computed LineTotal AS (Quantity * UnitPrice) PERSISTED.
Addresses records CustomerID, AddressType ('Billing' or 'Shipping'), and the street, city, state, and zip values.

Elements.Title: Foreign Key Constraints in the Schema
Elements.BodyText: Four named foreign key constraints wire the tables together and enforce referential integrity at the database level. Naming constraints explicitly makes errors and maintenance far easier to interpret.
Elements.Notes: Example: CONSTRAINT FK_OrderItems_Orders FOREIGN KEY (OrderID) REFERENCES Orders(OrderID).

Items.Text: FK_Orders_Customers links Orders.CustomerID to Customers.CustomerID.
FK_Addresses_Customers links Addresses.CustomerID to Customers.CustomerID.
FK_OrderItems_Orders links OrderItems.OrderID to Orders.OrderID.
FK_OrderItems_Products links OrderItems.ProductID to Products.ProductID.
All FK columns are declared NOT NULL, so every child row must point to a valid parent.
Use the FK_ChildTable_ParentTable naming convention so constraint violation messages identify the relationship immediately.

Elements.Title: Dependency-Level Thinking
Elements.BodyText: Grouping tables into dependency levels turns an abstract diagram into a concrete insert plan. A table's level is one higher than the highest level of any table it references.
Elements.Notes: Level 0: Customers, Products. Level 1: Orders (FK → Customers), Addresses (FK → Customers). Level 2: OrderItems (FK → Orders, FK → Products).

Items.Text: Level 0 tables have no foreign keys and can be populated at any time.
Level 1 tables depend only on Level 0 parents.
Level 2 tables depend on Level 1 parents and may also reference Level 0 tables directly.
OrderItems sits at Level 2 because it references Orders (Level 1), even though Products is Level 0.
Sketching this hierarchy before writing code prevents guesswork later.

Elements.Title: Deriving the Correct Insert Order
Elements.BodyText: Rows must always be inserted parent-first, moving from the lowest dependency level upward. Inserting a child before its parent raises a foreign key violation and aborts the statement.
Elements.Notes: A valid sequence for this schema: Customers → Addresses → Orders → OrderItems (with Products already populated as reference data).

Items.Text: Insert Level 0 rows first so their identity values exist to be referenced.
Capture each generated key with SCOPE_IDENTITY() before moving to the next level.
Tables at the same level have no ordering requirement relative to each other — Orders and Addresses can be inserted in either sequence.
Deletes run in the reverse direction: remove children before parents.
The usp_CreateCompleteOrder procedure follows exactly this order: Customer, then Address, then Order.

Elements.Title: Validating Parent Rows Before Inserting
Elements.BodyText: Even with the right ordering, a child insert can fail if the supplied parent key does not exist. Explicit validation produces clearer, more actionable errors than raw constraint violations.
Elements.Notes: Example: IF NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Customers WHERE CustomerID = @CustomerID) RAISERROR('Customer does not exist', 16, 1);

Items.Text: Check parent existence with IF NOT EXISTS before running the INSERT.
usp_InsertOrder validates the customer; usp_InsertOrderItem validates both the order and the product.
Looking up a value such as UnitPrice and testing it for NULL doubles as an existence check.
Validate inputs before opening a transaction so you avoid unnecessary rollbacks.
Return a negative status code alongside the error message so callers can branch on the result.

Elements.Title: Why Identity Columns Shape the Design
Elements.BodyText: Because every primary key in this schema is an identity column, child values cannot be known until the parent row is actually inserted. This is precisely what makes dependency order and key retrieval inseparable.
Elements.Notes: Identity values are never reused after a rollback, so gaps in the sequence are normal and expected.

Items.Text: IDENTITY(seed, increment) controls the starting value and step size — IDENTITY(1,1) yields 1, 2, 3; IDENTITY(1000,1) starts at 1000.
SQL Server guarantees uniqueness and handles concurrent inserts safely without application-level ID generation.
The generated key must be read back with SCOPE_IDENTITY() or the OUTPUT clause before the child insert can use it.
Index foreign key columns such as Orders.CustomerID and OrderItems.OrderID to keep joins and constraint checks fast.

Topics.Title: Building INSERT Stored Procedures
Topics.Summary: Demonstrates progressively complex insert procedures: a simple insert returning an identity value, a one-level foreign key insert with validation, and a multi-level insert that resolves related keys. Includes OUTPUT parameters and usage examples for calling each procedure.

Elements.Title: Procedure Structure and the OUTPUT Parameter Pattern
Elements.BodyText: Every insert procedure in this module follows the same skeleton: input parameters, SET NOCOUNT ON, validation, the INSERT, capture of the identity value, and a return code. OUTPUT parameters are the standard way to hand the newly generated key back to the caller.
Elements.Notes: Naming follows the usp_VerbNoun convention (usp_InsertCustomer, usp_InsertOrder, usp_InsertOrderItem) with @PascalCase parameters.

Items.Text: Declare the key-returning parameter with the OUTPUT keyword, for example @CustomerID INT OUTPUT.
SET NOCOUNT ON at the top suppresses extra 'rows affected' result sets that confuse calling applications.
Use SCOPE_IDENTITY() immediately after the INSERT to populate the OUTPUT parameter safely.
Return 0 for success and a negative value such as -1 to signal a validation failure.
The caller must also specify OUTPUT on the argument when executing the procedure, or the value comes back NULL.

Elements.Title: Simple Insert Returning an Identity Value
Elements.BodyText: The simplest case inserts into a table with no foreign key dependencies and returns the generated primary key. usp_InsertCustomer demonstrates this pattern against the Customers table.
Elements.Notes: Customers sits at Level 0 of the dependency hierarchy, so no parent validation is required.

Items.Text: Accept @FirstName, @LastName and @Email as inputs plus @CustomerID INT OUTPUT.
INSERT INTO Customers (FirstName, LastName, Email) VALUES (@FirstName, @LastName, @Email).
SET @CustomerID = SCOPE_IDENTITY() captures the value generated by that statement in the current scope.
Call it by declaring a local variable and passing it with the OUTPUT keyword: EXEC usp_InsertCustomer @FirstName = 'John', ..., @CustomerID = @NewCustomerID OUTPUT.
SELECT the local variable afterward to confirm the new key was returned.

Elements.Title: One-Level Foreign Key Insert with Validation
Elements.BodyText: When the target table references a parent, the procedure must confirm the parent row exists before inserting. usp_InsertOrder validates the customer, then creates the order and returns the new OrderID.
Elements.Notes: Validating before the INSERT produces a clearer error message than letting the foreign key constraint fire.

Items.Text: Use IF NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Customers WHERE CustomerID = @CustomerID) to test the parent key.
Raise a descriptive error with RAISERROR('Customer does not exist', 16, 1) and RETURN -1 to abort.
Insert CustomerID, GETDATE(), @TotalAmount and @Status into Orders once validation passes.
Capture SCOPE_IDENTITY() into @OrderID OUTPUT so the caller can add line items next.
Usage: DECLARE @NewOrderID INT; EXEC usp_InsertOrder @CustomerID = 1, @TotalAmount = 299.99, @Status = 'Pending', @OrderID = @NewOrderID OUTPUT.

Elements.Title: Multi-Level Insert Resolving Related Keys
Elements.BodyText: At the deepest level a row may depend on two different parents and may need to look up data from one of them. usp_InsertOrderItem validates the Order, validates the Product, and pulls the current UnitPrice from Products.
Elements.Notes: OrderItems is a Level 2 table with foreign keys to both Orders and Products; LineTotal is a computed persisted column so it is never inserted directly.

Items.Text: Validate the order first with IF NOT EXISTS against the Orders table.
Retrieve the price with SELECT @UnitPrice = UnitPrice FROM Products WHERE ProductID = @ProductID.
Test IF @UnitPrice IS NULL to detect a missing product — a single query serves as both lookup and existence check.
Insert OrderID, ProductID, Quantity and the resolved UnitPrice, then return @OrderItemID via SCOPE_IDENTITY().
Usage: EXEC usp_InsertOrderItem @OrderID = 1, @ProductID = 5, @Quantity = 2, @OrderItemID = @NewOrderItemID OUTPUT.

Elements.Title: Find-or-Create Logic for Lookup Parents
Elements.BodyText: A common variation inserts the parent only when it does not already exist, reusing the existing key otherwise. The Music Database sp_InsertSong procedure illustrates this find-or-create pattern across Artists, Albums and Songs.
Elements.Notes: The same pattern is required by the Menu/MenuGroups/MenuItems assignment: check MenuTitle, then MenuGroupText, then insert the MenuItem.

Items.Text: Count matching parent rows into a variable, for example SET @ArtistCount = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Artists WHERE Name = @ArtistName).
Use IF...ELSE with BEGIN/END blocks: if found, SELECT the existing ID; if not, INSERT and capture the new identity.
Repeat the same logic one level down, passing the resolved @ArtistID into the Albums insert.
Finish by inserting the child row (Songs) using the keys resolved in the previous steps.
Prefer SCOPE_IDENTITY() over @@IDENTITY in these procedures so triggers on the parent tables cannot return the wrong key.

Elements.Title: Chaining the Procedures Together
Elements.BodyText: Because each procedure returns its generated key through an OUTPUT parameter, the three levels can be called in sequence to build a complete order from scratch.
Elements.Notes: This layered approach keeps each procedure small and testable while still supporting complex multi-table inserts.

Items.Text: Call usp_InsertCustomer and hold the returned @CustID in a local variable.
Pass that value as @CustomerID into usp_InsertOrder and capture @OrdID.
Pass @OrdID into repeated calls of usp_InsertOrderItem, one per line item.
Check the procedure return code (0 = success, -1 = failure) after each EXEC before continuing.
SELECT the collected IDs at the end to verify the full hierarchy was created correctly.

Topics.Title: Transaction Management for Multi-Table Inserts
Topics.Summary: Shows how to wrap related inserts in explicit transactions with TRY...CATCH, XACT_ABORT, and @@TRANCOUNT checks so that all operations succeed or fail together. Covers nested transaction handling and transaction scope best practices.

Elements.Title: Why Transactions Matter for Related Inserts
Elements.BodyText: When a single logical operation spans several tables connected by foreign keys, partial success leaves the database in an inconsistent state. Explicit transactions guarantee that every insert in the sequence either commits together or is undone together.
Elements.Notes: Example: creating a customer, an address, and an order in usp_CreateCompleteOrder — if the order insert fails, the orphaned customer and address must not remain.

Items.Text: Always use explicit transactions when inserting data into parent and child tables in the same operation.
A transaction makes the multi-step insert atomic, so referential integrity is never left half-built.
Identity values consumed by a rolled-back insert are not reused, so gaps in identity sequences are normal.
Keep transactions as short as possible to minimize locking and blocking for other sessions.
Validate inputs before BEGIN TRANSACTION whenever possible so failures happen outside the transaction scope.

Elements.Title: The BEGIN TRY / BEGIN TRANSACTION Pattern
Elements.BodyText: The standard T-SQL structure wraps BEGIN TRANSACTION and all inserts inside a BEGIN TRY block, with COMMIT TRANSACTION as the last statement before END TRY. The matching BEGIN CATCH block performs the rollback and error reporting.
Elements.Notes: In usp_CreateCompleteOrder the procedure inserts Customer, then Address, then Order, capturing SCOPE_IDENTITY() after each insert before committing.

Items.Text: Open with SET NOCOUNT ON, then BEGIN TRY followed immediately by BEGIN TRANSACTION.
Perform each dependent insert in dependency order, capturing SCOPE_IDENTITY() for the next level's foreign key.
Place COMMIT TRANSACTION as the final action inside the TRY block and RETURN 0 to signal success.
Any error raised inside the TRY block transfers control straight to the CATCH block, skipping the COMMIT.
Return a negative status code from the CATCH block so the caller can distinguish success from failure.

Elements.Title: Checking @@TRANCOUNT Before ROLLBACK
Elements.BodyText: @@TRANCOUNT reports how many transactions are currently open on the connection. Testing it before issuing ROLLBACK prevents a secondary error when no transaction is actually active.
Elements.Notes: Pattern: IF @@TRANCOUNT > 0 ROLLBACK TRANSACTION;

Items.Text: Issuing ROLLBACK with no open transaction raises its own error and masks the original failure.
Every CATCH block in the examples begins with IF @@TRANCOUNT > 0 ROLLBACK TRANSACTION.
Some errors (especially with XACT_ABORT ON) already roll the transaction back before CATCH runs, leaving @@TRANCOUNT at zero.
Not checking @@TRANCOUNT before ROLLBACK is listed among the most common stored procedure pitfalls.
After rolling back, capture ERROR_MESSAGE(), ERROR_SEVERITY(), and ERROR_STATE() and re-raise with RAISERROR or THROW.

Elements.Title: Using SET XACT_ABORT ON
Elements.BodyText: SET XACT_ABORT ON instructs SQL Server to automatically terminate and roll back the entire transaction when a run-time error occurs. It is a safety net for errors that would otherwise leave a transaction open.
Elements.Notes: usp_CreateOrderWithItems uses SET XACT_ABORT ON at the top; usp_InsertOrderWithErrorHandling deliberately sets it OFF to handle validation errors explicitly.

Items.Text: Place SET XACT_ABORT ON immediately after SET NOCOUNT ON at the start of the procedure.
It guarantees no partially completed transaction survives an unhandled statement-level error.
Use SET XACT_ABORT OFF when you want to raise validation errors and control rollback behavior yourself.
Even with XACT_ABORT ON, keep the TRY...CATCH block for error logging and re-throwing to the caller.
Combine XACT_ABORT with the @@TRANCOUNT check so the rollback logic is correct in either configuration.

Elements.Title: Nested Transaction Handling
Elements.BodyText: A stored procedure may be called from another procedure that already started a transaction. The procedure should only begin and commit a transaction if it is the one that opened it.
Elements.Notes: Pattern from usp_NestedTransactionExample: DECLARE @TransactionStarted BIT = 0; IF @@TRANCOUNT = 0 BEGIN TRANSACTION; SET @TransactionStarted = 1; END

Items.Text: Declare a flag variable such as @TransactionStarted BIT = 0 to record whether this procedure opened the transaction.
Only call BEGIN TRANSACTION when @@TRANCOUNT = 0, then set the flag to 1.
Commit only when the flag is 1, so an outer caller retains control of its own transaction.
In the CATCH block, roll back only when the flag is 1 AND @@TRANCOUNT > 0.
Use THROW to re-raise the error to the caller so the outer transaction can decide how to respond.

Elements.Title: Transaction Scope Best Practices
Elements.BodyText: Good transaction design keeps the protected region narrow, predictable, and well tested. These guidelines apply to every multi-table insert procedure you write.
Elements.Notes: Testing should include valid data, invalid data, rollback scenarios, and concurrent execution to confirm the transaction behaves as designed.

Items.Text: Wrap only the operations that must succeed or fail together — avoid long-running work inside the transaction.
Use an appropriate isolation level; READ COMMITTED is usually sufficient for insert workflows.
Perform existence checks and parameter validation before opening the transaction where practical.
Log errors to an ErrorLog table from the CATCH block, then THROW to preserve the original error for the caller.
Explicitly test rollback paths to verify that no partial rows remain after a simulated failure.

Topics.Title: Error Handling, Validation, and Logging
Topics.Summary: Presents a comprehensive validation and error-handling pattern using RAISERROR, THROW, return codes, and OUTPUT error messages. Includes building an ErrorLog table and a reusable logging procedure for diagnostics.

Elements.Title: Validate Inputs Before Touching Data
Elements.BodyText: Defensive stored procedures check every assumption about foreign keys and business rules before any INSERT occurs. Validation up front avoids wasted work and constraint violations deep inside a transaction.
Elements.Notes: In usp_InsertOrderWithErrorHandling, four validations run before the first INSERT: customer exists, product exists, quantity is positive, and stock is sufficient.

Items.Text: Use IF NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Customers WHERE CustomerID = @CustomerID) to confirm parent rows exist.
Capture lookup values during validation, such as SELECT @UnitPrice = UnitPrice FROM Products, then test IF @UnitPrice IS NULL.
Enforce business rules like IF @Quantity <= 0 or insufficient StockQuantity before committing resources.
Validate inputs before beginning transactions so locks are held for the shortest possible time.
Build messages that name the offending value, for example 'Customer ID ' + CAST(@CustomerID AS NVARCHAR) + ' not found'.

Elements.Title: Raising Errors with RAISERROR and THROW
Elements.BodyText: T-SQL offers two ways to signal failure: RAISERROR, which supports formatted messages and explicit severity/state, and THROW, which re-raises the original error intact.
Elements.Notes: Severity 16 is the conventional level for user-correctable errors; it transfers control to the CATCH block inside a TRY.

Items.Text: RAISERROR('Customer does not exist', 16, 1) raises a custom message with severity 16 and state 1.
RAISERROR supports substitution tokens, as in RAISERROR('Customer ID %d does not exist', 16, 1, @CustomerID).
THROW with no arguments inside CATCH re-raises the original error number, message, and line to the caller.
Use THROW when the caller should see the native error; use RAISERROR when you need a custom message or severity.
Never expose sensitive data such as connection details or private values inside error messages.

Elements.Title: TRY...CATCH With Transaction-Safe Rollback
Elements.BodyText: Every procedure that performs related inserts should wrap its work in BEGIN TRY / BEGIN CATCH and guard the rollback with a transaction count check.
Elements.Notes: CATCH blocks can read ERROR_NUMBER(), ERROR_MESSAGE(), ERROR_SEVERITY(), ERROR_STATE(), ERROR_LINE(), and ERROR_PROCEDURE().

Items.Text: Place BEGIN TRANSACTION immediately inside BEGIN TRY and COMMIT TRANSACTION as the last statement of the try block.
Always test IF @@TRANCOUNT > 0 before issuing ROLLBACK TRANSACTION to avoid a second error.
SET XACT_ABORT ON forces automatic rollback on errors; SET XACT_ABORT OFF lets you handle failures explicitly.
For nested calls, track a @TransactionStarted BIT flag so only the procedure that opened the transaction commits or rolls it back.
Re-throw captured values with RAISERROR(@ErrorMessage, @ErrorSeverity, @ErrorState) to preserve context for the caller.

Elements.Title: Return Codes and OUTPUT Error Messages
Elements.BodyText: A stored procedure can communicate outcome two ways at once: a numeric RETURN code for status and OUTPUT parameters for identity values and human-readable error text.
Elements.Notes: Convention: RETURN 0 for success, negative values such as -1 for errors.

Items.Text: Declare @ErrorMessage NVARCHAR(4000) OUTPUT alongside @OrderID INT OUTPUT to return both diagnostics and results.
On success, set the error OUTPUT to NULL and RETURN 0; on failure, set identity OUTPUTs to NULL and RETURN -1.
Compose a rich message in CATCH: 'Error ' + CAST(ERROR_NUMBER() AS NVARCHAR) + ': ' + ERROR_MESSAGE() + ' (Line ' + CAST(ERROR_LINE() AS NVARCHAR) + ')'.
Callers capture status with EXEC @ReturnCode = usp_InsertOrderWithErrorHandling ... and branch on IF @ReturnCode = 0.
Reset counters and IDs, such as SET @RecordsCreated = 0, so partial results are never mistaken for success.

Elements.Title: Building an ErrorLog Table
Elements.BodyText: Persisting error details to a dedicated table turns transient failures into a searchable diagnostic history.
Elements.Notes: Because the log INSERT happens after a ROLLBACK, the log row survives even when the business transaction is undone.

Items.Text: Create ErrorLog with an IDENTITY primary key plus ErrorNumber, ErrorSeverity, and ErrorState columns.
Record context columns ErrorProcedure NVARCHAR(128), ErrorLine INT, and ErrorMessage NVARCHAR(4000).
Add ErrorDate DATETIME DEFAULT GETDATE() so each entry is automatically timestamped.
Keep the table free of foreign keys and constraints so logging never fails for its own reasons.
Query the log to spot recurring validation failures, problem procedures, and error hotspots by line number.

Elements.Title: A Reusable usp_LogError Procedure
Elements.BodyText: Centralizing the logging INSERT in one procedure keeps CATCH blocks short and guarantees consistent diagnostics across the whole database.
Elements.Notes: The ERROR_* functions remain valid inside a procedure called from a CATCH block, which is what makes this pattern work.

Items.Text: usp_LogError starts with SET NOCOUNT ON and inserts the six ERROR_* function values into ErrorLog.
It takes no parameters because it reads the ambient error context of the calling CATCH block.
The standard usage is BEGIN CATCH EXEC usp_LogError; THROW; END CATCH — log first, then re-raise.
Logging before THROW ensures the record is written even if the caller swallows the exception.
Reusing one procedure means a change to the log schema requires edits in only one place.

Elements.Title: Error Handling Standards and Pitfalls
Elements.BodyText: Consistent conventions make error handling predictable for every developer and every calling application.
Elements.Notes: Also test deliberately: invalid data, rollback scenarios, NULL inputs, and concurrent execution.

Items.Text: Always use TRY...CATCH, check @@TRANCOUNT before ROLLBACK, and write meaningful messages with RAISERROR or THROW.
Return status codes (0 success, negative for errors) and consider OUTPUT parameters for error text.
Log errors to an error table for diagnostics rather than relying on client-side capture alone.
Avoid the pitfalls of inadequate logging, unchecked rollbacks, and transactions left open too long.
Document each procedure's return values and parameters in a header comment so callers know how to interpret failures.

Topics.Title: Advanced Techniques: Batch Inserts and Table-Valued Parameters
Topics.Summary: Covers creating user-defined table types and passing multiple rows into a procedure with READONLY table-valued parameters. Also shows the OUTPUT clause for capturing multiple inserted rows and composing complete orders in a single call.

Elements.Title: Why Table-Valued Parameters?
Elements.BodyText: Table-valued parameters (TVPs) let you pass multiple rows of data into a stored procedure in a single call, making them ideal for batch inserts across foreign key relationships.
Elements.Notes: Before TVPs, developers passed delimited strings or XML, or made one procedure call per row — both approaches are slower and harder to maintain.

Items.Text: TVPs reduce network round-trips by sending an entire set of rows at once.
They improve performance compared to looping single-row INSERT calls from the application.
Code becomes more maintainable than parsing delimited strings inside T-SQL.
They pair naturally with multi-table inserts where a parent row drives many child rows.
Best practice guidance explicitly recommends TVPs for batch inserts.

Elements.Title: Creating User-Defined Table Types
Elements.BodyText: A TVP must be based on a user-defined table type created with CREATE TYPE ... AS TABLE. The type defines the columns and data types of the rows you intend to pass.
Elements.Notes: Example: CREATE TYPE OrderItemType AS TABLE (ProductID INT NOT NULL, Quantity INT NOT NULL); and CREATE TYPE AddressType AS TABLE (AddressType NVARCHAR(20), StreetAddress NVARCHAR(200), City NVARCHAR(100), State NVARCHAR(50), ZipCode NVARCHAR(20));

Items.Text: Define only the columns the caller supplies — omit identity and foreign key columns the procedure will generate.
OrderItemType carries just ProductID and Quantity; the procedure looks up UnitPrice itself.
NOT NULL constraints on type columns provide a first line of input validation.
Follow the NounType naming convention (e.g., OrderItemType, AddressType).
The type must exist in the database before any procedure that references it is created.

Elements.Title: Declaring READONLY TVP Parameters
Elements.BodyText: Inside a stored procedure, a table-valued parameter is declared with the table type name followed by the READONLY keyword, which is mandatory for TVPs.
Elements.Notes: Example: @OrderItems OrderItemType READONLY alongside normal scalar parameters such as @CustomerID and an @OrderID INT OUTPUT.

Items.Text: READONLY means the procedure cannot INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE rows in the parameter.
You can freely SELECT from, JOIN to, and aggregate over the TVP as if it were a table variable.
TVPs can be mixed with ordinary scalar input parameters and OUTPUT parameters.
Omitting READONLY causes a compile-time error when creating the procedure.

Elements.Title: Populating and Calling with a TVP
Elements.BodyText: Callers declare a variable of the table type, insert rows into it, then pass it as a parameter on the EXEC statement.
Elements.Notes: Example: DECLARE @Items OrderItemType; INSERT INTO @Items (ProductID, Quantity) VALUES (1,2),(3,1),(5,3); EXEC usp_CreateOrderWithItemsTVP @CustomerID = 1, @Status = 'Pending', @OrderItems = @Items, @OrderID = @NewOrderID OUTPUT;

Items.Text: Declare the variable using the user-defined type name, not a column list.
Use a multi-row VALUES clause to load several items in a single INSERT.
Pass the table variable by name just like any other named parameter.
The procedure still returns the generated OrderID through an OUTPUT parameter.
From application code, a TVP maps to a DataTable or structured SqlParameter.

Elements.Title: Set-Based Validation and Insertion Inside the Procedure
Elements.BodyText: Because a TVP behaves like a table, validation and insertion can be done with set-based statements instead of row-by-row loops.
Elements.Notes: The usp_CreateOrderWithItemsTVP example validates the customer, validates all products, computes the total, inserts the order, then inserts all items in one statement — all wrapped in BEGIN TRY / BEGIN TRANSACTION with THROW in the CATCH.

Items.Text: LEFT JOIN the TVP to Products and test for NULL to detect any invalid ProductID in one check.
Compute the order total with SUM(oi.Quantity * p.UnitPrice) joined across the TVP and Products.
Insert the parent Orders row first and capture SCOPE_IDENTITY() into @OrderID.
Insert every child row with a single INSERT ... SELECT that joins the TVP to Products and uses @OrderID.
Wrap the whole sequence in a transaction so the order and all its items commit or roll back together.

Elements.Title: Capturing Multiple Inserted Rows with the OUTPUT Clause
Elements.BodyText: When a single INSERT creates many rows, SCOPE_IDENTITY() returns only the last value; the OUTPUT clause captures every generated key and column instead.
Elements.Notes: Example: INSERT INTO OrderItems (...) OUTPUT inserted.OrderItemID, inserted.ProductID, inserted.Quantity, inserted.LineTotal INTO @InsertedItems SELECT ... FROM Products WHERE ProductID IN (1,2,3); then SELECT * FROM @InsertedItems;

Items.Text: Declare a table variable whose columns match the OUTPUT column list.
Reference the virtual inserted table to pull back identity values and computed columns such as LineTotal.
OUTPUT is statement-scoped, trigger-safe and concurrency-safe, unlike @@IDENTITY.
The captured rows can be returned to the caller as a result set or used for further processing.
Use SCOPE_IDENTITY() for single-row inserts and OUTPUT for multi-row inserts.

Elements.Title: Composing a Complete Order in a Single Call
Elements.BodyText: Advanced procedures combine TVPs, OUTPUT parameters, and transactions to create a customer, address, order, and all line items in one atomic call.
Elements.Notes: usp_CreateCompleteOrder accepts customer, address, and order details and returns @CustomerID, @OrderID and @AddressID as OUTPUT parameters, chaining SCOPE_IDENTITY() from each insert to the next.

Items.Text: Each SCOPE_IDENTITY() value becomes the foreign key for the next insert in the chain.
Multiple OUTPUT parameters return every generated key to the caller in one round-trip.
A TRY...CATCH block rolls back when @@TRANCOUNT > 0 and re-raises the error.
On failure, set OUTPUT parameters to NULL so callers cannot mistake partial results for success.
Document the procedure header with parameters, return codes, and a usage example for maintainability.

Topics.Title: Evaluating Approaches and Professional Best Practices
Topics.Summary: Weighs stored procedures against ORM (Entity Framework), ADO.NET, and hybrid approaches across performance, maintainability, testability, and portability. Concludes with naming, performance, security, documentation, testing standards, and common pitfalls to avoid.

Elements.Title: Strengths and Trade-offs of the Stored Procedure Approach
Elements.BodyText: Stored procedures centralize multi-table insert logic inside the database, but that power comes with costs that must be weighed before standardizing on them.
Elements.Notes: Advantages: data integrity, compiled execution plans, reduced network traffic, parameterization against SQL injection, centralized reusable business logic, built-in transaction support, and abstraction of schema complexity. Considerations: T-SQL vendor lock-in, migration tooling needs, SQL expertise requirements, database-dependent integration tests, weaker debugging tools, and less dynamic flexibility than an ORM.

Items.Text: Encapsulating foreign key workflows guarantees atomicity and referential integrity across Customers, Orders, and OrderItems.
Execution plan reuse and a single round-trip per operation deliver strong performance for bulk and multi-table work.
Granting EXECUTE on procedures instead of direct table access tightens the security surface.
Costs include SQL Server lock-in, a steeper learning curve, complex deployments, and limited debugging compared to application code.

Elements.Title: Deciding When a Stored Procedure Is the Right Tool
Elements.BodyText: Not every data operation belongs in a stored procedure; the decision depends on complexity, volume, and how often the rules change.
Elements.Notes: Use the scenario matrix as a quick triage guide rather than an absolute rule.

Items.Text: Use procedures for complex multi-table inserts where atomicity and referential integrity matter most.
Use procedures for bulk operations and centralized business-rule validation to cut network traffic and ensure consistency.
Simple single-table CRUD and dynamic filtering or searching are often simpler and more flexible in an ORM.
Frequently changing business rules may belong in application code, which is easier to modify, test, and redeploy.

Elements.Title: Alternative 1: ORM-Based Inserts with Entity Framework
Elements.BodyText: Entity Framework can manage the same parent-child insert sequence in C#, using an explicit transaction and successive SaveChanges() calls to obtain generated keys.
Elements.Notes: Example: add a Customer, call SaveChanges() to populate customer.CustomerID, then use that value on the new Order, and finally AddRange the OrderItems before committing.

Items.Text: context.Database.BeginTransaction() wraps the whole sequence so a failure can be rolled back in the catch block.
Each SaveChanges() call materializes the identity value back onto the entity object for use as a foreign key.
EF offers excellent maintainability, testability, and portability plus an easy learning curve.
The trade-off is additional round-trips and less control over the generated SQL than a single procedure call.

Elements.Title: Alternative 2: Application-Level Logic with ADO.NET
Elements.BodyText: Raw ADO.NET gives fine-grained control by issuing parameterized INSERT statements that use the OUTPUT clause to return generated identity values.
Elements.Notes: Example: INSERT INTO Customers ... OUTPUT INSERTED.CustomerID ... VALUES (@FirstName, @LastName, @Email), retrieved with ExecuteScalar().

Items.Text: SqlConnection and SqlTransaction coordinate commit and rollback across multiple commands.
OUTPUT INSERTED.CustomerID with ExecuteScalar() returns the new key without a separate SELECT.
Always use SqlParameter values rather than string concatenation to prevent SQL injection.
Performance is very good and flexibility is high, but there is far more boilerplate code to maintain.

Elements.Title: Alternative 3: The Hybrid Approach and Comparison Matrix
Elements.BodyText: Many production systems combine approaches: an ORM handles simple CRUD while stored procedures handle complex, high-value transactions.
Elements.Notes: EF can invoke a procedure directly via context.Database.ExecuteSqlCommand with SqlParameter objects whose Direction is set to ParameterDirection.Output, then read the generated IDs from .Value.

Items.Text: Stored procedures rate highest on performance, security, and atomic multi-table control, but lowest on portability.
ORMs rate highest on maintainability, testability, flexibility, and ease of learning.
Application logic sits between the two, offering very good performance with moderate portability.
Calling usp_CreateCompleteOrder from EF with OUTPUT parameters captures CustomerID and OrderID in a single round-trip.

Elements.Title: Professional Standards: Naming, Performance, and Security
Elements.BodyText: Consistent conventions and defensive coding habits make procedures predictable, fast, and safe to expose to applications.
Elements.Notes: Naming: usp_VerbNoun for procedures (usp_InsertOrder, usp_GetCustomerOrders), @PascalCase for parameters and locals, and NounType for user-defined table types (OrderItemType, AddressType).

Items.Text: Always start procedures with SET NOCOUNT ON and prefer SCOPE_IDENTITY() over @@IDENTITY.
Keep transaction scope minimal, index foreign key columns, and use table-valued parameters for batch inserts.
Grant EXECUTE on procedures instead of direct table permissions and run under least-privilege service accounts.
Validate every input parameter, avoid dynamic SQL (use sp_executesql if unavoidable), and never leak sensitive data in error messages.

Elements.Title: Documentation, Testing, and Common Pitfalls
Elements.BodyText: A professional procedure ships with a header comment block, a repeatable test plan, and deliberate avoidance of well-known mistakes.
Elements.Notes: A standard header documents the procedure name, description, each parameter, the return codes (0 success, -1 error), a runnable usage example, and a dated change history.

Items.Text: Test valid data, invalid data, rollback scenarios, concurrency, NULL inputs, and realistic data volumes.
Verify that foreign key constraints are enforced and that identity values are returned correctly to the caller.
Avoid @@IDENTITY, rolling back without checking @@TRANCOUNT, and leaving transactions open too long.
Avoid skipping SET NOCOUNT ON, omitting OUTPUT parameters for generated IDs, weak error logging, and hardcoding values that should be parameters.
